added_lines: parish of the holy family aughrim street parish bulletin 18 october 2026 in this sunday’s gospel, the pharisees once again were tr ying to trick jesus with their question. but his reply was sharp, to the point, yet in its directness put an end to the pharisees’ duplicity. we can all be cunning like the pharisees, not only towards others , but towards ourselves too. we can focus on non-essentials, over- complicate our lives with the things that don’t matter, the things that draw us away from o ur relationship with god. we can be mesmerised by wealth and power, even jealous of those who appear to have more than we have. we long for material treats and lose sight of our gifts from god. the gospel puts us firmly back on the right road in our journey to god. it’s a journey of simplicity and a journey in which we leave a light footprint on the world and on others. when we strip away the non- essentials, we have a wonderful and sometimes challenging opportunity to love and be loved. in today’s gospel, we are invited to be less like the pharisees and consciously reduce the number of times we try to trip others up, cut back on the rash comments and actively choose kind, uplifting words. but we should probably first try to stop tripping ourselves up! you hypocrites! why do you set this trap for me? aughrim street

10.30am mass, church of the holy child, whitehall opening hymn no.8 closing hymn no.32 hymns whose image do we bear? we bear? whose image do we bear? “each of us is the result of a thought of god. each of us is willed, each of us is loved, each of us is necessary.” pope benedict xvi thought for the week dates for your diary we pay our dues to the world readily enough. do we give our whole hearts to the god whose image we bear? to ponder this week in the gospel, the pharisees and herodians attempt to trap jesus with a politically charged question: "is it permissible to pay taxes to caesar or not?" instead of falling into their political snare, jesus calls for a denarius and asks, "whose head is this? whose inscription?". when they reply, "caesar's," he delivers a timeless truth: "give back to caesar what belongs to caesar—and to god what belongs to god." holy child nativity parishes beaumont | larkhill | whitehall | santry jesus does not separate church and state; rather, he distinguishes a hierarchy of authority. while the coin carries caesar’s likeness and currency, human beings carry the indelible image and likeness of god. this means that while civil authority has a legitimate place, our ultimate obedience, our hearts, and our very lives belong entirely to our creator. this divine sovereignty is echoed in the first reading from isaiah 45. the lord uses cyrus, a pagan persian king, as an instrument to free the exiled israelites. god reminds us that he is the ultimate master of history: "i am the lord, unrivalled; there is no other god besides he readings for this sunday invite us to look beyond our worldly commitments and remember our truest identity. year a | 29 sunday in ordinary time th
